passages.t: ‘In God alone my soul finds rest’
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. According to Jeduthun. A Psalm of David” (verse 1). The psalm opens in quiet confidence. “In God alone my soul finds rest; my salvation comes from Him. He alone is my rock and my salvation. He is my fortress; I will never be shaken” (verses 1 and 2).

Around him are people trying to push him over, “like a leaning wall or a tottering fence” (verse 3). They are two-faced: “with their mouths they bless, but inwardly they curse” (verse 4).

Then he speaks to himself, as Psalm 42 did. “Rest in God alone, O my soul, for my hope comes from Him” (verse 5). And he turns to everyone else. “Trust in Him at all times, O people; pour out your hearts before Him. God is our refuge” (verse 8).

People, high or low, weigh almost nothing (verse 9). Money cannot be trusted either. “If your riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (verse 10). The psalm ends with two things God has said: power belongs to God, and “loving devotion to You, O Lord” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Jeduthun was one of the music leaders of David's time, and his name also heads Psalms 39 and 77. The book page explains such names.

One small Hebrew word runs through this psalm. It is ‘akh, which means ‘only’, ‘alone’ or ‘surely’. It comes six times (verses 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 9). The BSB often puts it as ‘alone’. The psalm keeps saying: God, and only God.

The word in verse 1 that gives ‘finds rest’ is, more exactly, ‘silence’. ‘My soul is silent toward God’ means the struggling stops. It is the quiet of trust.

Walls were often built of mudbrick or rough stone without mortar. A leaning one would soon fall. In verse 9 people are put on a merchant's scales, and the pan goes up because they weigh nothing. The word is hevel, ‘breath’ or ‘vapour’, the same word that runs through Ecclesiastes.
passages.later:
Jesus warned, “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy” (Matthew 6:19).

Verse 12 is quoted by Paul: God “will repay each one according to his deeds” (Romans 2:6). Paul uses it to say that God judges fairly, Jew and Gentile alike.
passages.asks:
‘Rest’ here is not doing nothing. It is stopping the inner struggle and trusting God with it. The psalmist has to tell his own soul to do it, which means it did not come easily to him either.

Verse 8 is an invitation: ‘pour out your hearts before Him.’ Not tidy prayers. Everything. Then verse 10 asks a quiet question: what are you leaning your heart on that weighs less than a breath?
